Hauterive
oht-REEV
n. (the Cistercian abbey near Fribourg, founded 1138, still a living community)
French haute rive, the high bank, of the Sarine; Latin Altaripa.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hauterive stands on a bend of the Sarine south of Fribourg and was founded in 1138 by Guillaume de Glâne, settled from Cherlieu. Its church, consecrated in 1160, keeps its Cistercian plan; the cloister was rebuilt in the fourteenth century and holds some of the best Gothic glass in Switzerland. The house was suppressed by the canton in 1848 and the buildings used as a teachers' college, but monks returned in 1939 and Hauterive is a working abbey today, one of the few medieval Swiss houses with an unbroken community again in its own cloister. This dictionary records Hauterive for the return, which is a biblical motion rather than a sentimental one. Scripture treats the rebuilding of what was thrown down as God's own promise, “they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4), and Nehemiah makes it a work to be organised rather than merely desired, “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Neh 2:17). The affection that drives it is for the stones themselves, “For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof” (Psa 102:14), and the building that matters is never the masonry, “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to restore as to bring back to a former state; a ruin as the remains of a decayed building; to rebuild as to build again; desolation as a place laid waste; and perseverance as persistence in a course begun.

expand to see more

RESTORE, v.t. To return to a person, as a specific thing which he has lost; to bring back; to heal; to bring back to a former state.

RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; also, in the plural, the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men.

REBUILD, v.t. To build again; to repair or restore any thing that has been demolished or thrown down.

DESOLATION, n. The act of desolating; destruction of inhabitants; a place deprived of inhabitants or otherwise wasted.

PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken; continuance in a state of grace to the end.

Key Scripture

Isa 61:4 — "And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations."

Neh 2:17 — "Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach."

Psa 102:14 — "For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof."

Psa 127:1 — "A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain."

Modern Corruption

Swiss Cistercian abbey of 1138: suppressed in 1848, a teachers' college for ninety years, and a living community again since 1939.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that restoration is a work God names and claims. Isaiah does not promise that the ruins will be admired; he promises that they will be built, with generations of desolation reversed, “they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations” (Isa 61:4). Nehemiah's contribution is to say it out loud to people who had grown used to rubble, “Ye see the distress that we are in” (Neh 2:17).

The second thing is the affection that makes restoration possible. The psalm does not say the servants pleaded the strategic importance of Zion; it says they loved its broken stones and even its dust, “and favour the dust thereof” (Psa 102:14). That is what brought monks back to Hauterive in 1939 after ninety years. The caution is in the next psalm quoted, which refuses to let the builders congratulate themselves, “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; Hebrew chorbah (H2723), a waste place; Hebrew ratsah (H7521), to take pleasure in; Hebrew 'aphar (H6083), dust; Hebrew shaw' (H7723), in vain.

expand to see more

Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a ruin, a waste to be rebuilt; “they shall build the old wastes”, Isaiah 61:4.

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, to rebuild a wall; “let us build up the wall of Jerusalem”, Nehemiah 2:17.

Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to delight in; “thy servants take pleasure in her stones”, Psalm 102:14.

Hebrew 'aphar (H6083) — dust, loved for the place's sake; “and favour the dust thereof”, Psalm 102:14.

Hebrew shaw' (H7723) — emptiness, labour to no purpose; “they labour in vain that build it”, Psalm 127:1.

Usage

"“they shall build the old wastes” (Isa 61:4) — restoration promised, not merely hoped."

"“thy servants take pleasure in her stones” (Psa 102:14) — the affection that brings people back."

"“Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1) — the clause that keeps a restoration humble."
